title: London museum crash driver released by police as enquiries go on
text: British police said on Sunday that a man arrested after a car hit pedestrians in London, injuring 11, had been released under investigation while enquiries continued. The 47-year-old was arrested at the scene near London's Natural History Museum on Saturday on suspicion of dangerous driving. He was treated in hospital and then taken to a north London police station, the Metropolitan Police said. "This morning he was released under investigation while enquiries continue," the police said. People released under investigation do not have to return to a police station but can be contacted, and in some cases arrested again, following further police enquiries. A vehicle mounted the pavement and struck pedestrians in one of the capital's busiest tourist areas on Saturday afternoon, but police dismissed concerns that it was a terrorist attack. "Because of where this collision occurred and the number of pedestrians involved, I fully appreciate the concern and alarm this incident caused," DC Darren Case of the Roads and Transport Policing Command said on Sunday. "Enquiries have established that this incident is not terrorist related ... Thankfully there are no serious injuries with the majority now discharged from hospital."

title: U.S. welcomes Saudi-led coalition decision to keep Yemen port open
text: The United States said on Thursday it welcomed a Saudi-led coalition's announcement that it would keep Yemen's Hodeidah port open for a month to let humanitarian aid through, and it condemned a Houthi bombing of a palace in Saudi Arabia. In a short statement, White House spokeswoman Sarah Sanders indicated that the United States believed Iran bore ultimate responsibility for the Dec. 19 missile attack on the palace in Riyadh. "We urge the United Nations Security Council to hold Iran responsible for its repeated and blatant violations of Security Council resolutions," Sanders said. At a briefing later on Thursday, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Tim Lenderking said the United States would talk with Saudi Arabia about the 30 days the port will be open and about possibly changing that timeline, but said Washington first wants to see ships moving in and goods and services reaching the people of Yemen. The Saudi-led Arab coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it would open the Houthi-controlled port it had blockaded. A cholera epidemic has been spreading across the country, and 8 million people are on the brink of famine in what the United Nations considers the world's worst humanitarian crisis. The Saudis say the Red Sea port is also a hub the Houthis use to bring in weapons, which they accuse Iran of supplying. Tehran denies the charges. Lenderking also said there was no military solution to the conflict and that President Donald Trump's administration believes aggressive diplomacy is the best course. Trump had threatened to cut off financial aid to countries that voted on Thursday for a United Nations General Assembly resolution calling on the United States to drop its recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital.

title: Sweden says Congo is not helping probe into murder of U.N. monitor
text: Swedish prosecutors on Wednesday accused the government of Democratic Republic of Congo of failing to cooperate with their investigation into the murder of a U.N. sanctions monitor from Sweden. Zaida Catalan and her American colleague, Michael Sharp, were shot dead in March and found in a shallow grave in central Congo, in an area where they had been collecting information on a conflict between the army and a militia. Congo's government has arrested more than a dozen people in connection with the killings, which it blames on the militia, although one report to the U.N. Security Council suggested state security services might also be involved. The Swedish Prosecution Authority opened its own investigation into Catalan's death and said on Wednesday it had received no reply to a request for information it sent to Congolese authorities in April. "The Swedish investigation is facing severe difficulties given the fact that it is completely reliant on evidence that exists in the Congo and cooperation is not working with Congo," prosecutor Sara Nilsson said in the statement. Material that Swedish authorities had managed to gather does not rule out that people with close ties to the regime in Congo are involved in the murders, the Authority added. In April, Congo's government showed reporters a video that it said showed militia members killing Catalan and Sharp. But analysts said the grainy footage raised more questions than it answered, and Nilsson said the screening had tainted important evidence. Congo's government spokesman Lambert Mende has denied that Congolese officials were involved in the murders and said on Wednesday it was up to Swedish authorities to provide information to the Congolese court hearing the case, not the other way around.

title: With A Single Tweet, Elizabeth Warren Lays Down The Plain Truth About This Week’s Killings
text: If there's one lesson to take from the horrific shootings of this past week, it's that we, as a society, need more understanding and compassion for one another. No one deserves to die, especially not just for existing, or for protecting your community. Two black men were shot and killed by police officers who didn't even try to keep them alive, for reasons still to be determined, and five police officers were shot and killed, with seven more wounded, while serving and protecting protesters who were out voicing their concern about police brutality. Plenty of people have been offering their opinions on the violence, but one voice of reason seems to get right to the heart of what needs to be heard: the voice of Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA). The simple yet solid truth about all the killings of the past week was summed up in a tweet by Warren on July 8, 2016: "Black Americans shouldn't be killed in routine traffic stops, & police shouldn't be killed while protecting & serving their communities." It's really that simple. We can be on both sides of this issue without being against the other side. We can have compassion for the right of Black Americans to exist without fear of being shot and killed by the police, and we can also have compassion for police officers who are simply trying to protect the community they serve. We need to stand up to and against violence wherever it is, period.

title: Carnegie Hall Gets a New Leader With a Son Named Hendrix
text: Robert F. Smith, the private equity titan whom Forbes named the richest man last year after he made a fortune in software, also has a quirky musical side. He owns one of Elton John's old pianos. He hired John Legend and Seal, along with a youth orchestra, to perform at his wedding on the Amalfi Coast last summer. His youngest sons, Hendrix and Legend, are named for Jimi Hendrix and Mr. Legend. And he bought and restored a retreat in the Rocky Mountains that was beloved by jazz musicians, including Duke Ellington. On Thursday, Mr. Smith's overlapping worlds of money, philanthropy and music came together when he was named chairman of Carnegie Hall, the nation's most prestigious concert stage. He became the first to hold the post at a time when diversity at leading cultural organizations lags: a recent survey of New York's cultural institutions found that nearly 78 percent of their board members were white. “Carnegie Hall is perfectly placed to champion not only artistic excellence, but also access and exposure to the best music in the world,” Mr. Smith said in a statement. The election of Mr. Smith, 53, who played an old upright piano as a child in Denver and was told that with enough practice he might make it to Carnegie one day, ends a low moment at the hall. The billionaire Ronald O. Perelman served as its chairman for less than a year before stepping down last fall, after he alienated the board by clashing with the hall's executive and artistic director, Clive Gillinson. Mr. Smith, who is based in Austin, Tex., had shunned the spotlight for years.

title: Obama administration moves to strengthen fight against gender wage gap
text: The Obama administration on Friday announced plans to expand wage reporting requirements for private businesses, stepping up its efforts to narrow the longstanding U.S. gender wage gap. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's plan would require employers with 100 or more employees to give the agency detailed wage information broken down by gender, race and ethnicity. Unlike a similar Labor Department rule proposed earlier, it would cover all large businesses rather than only federal contractors. The plan, expected to take effect in September 2017, will be open to public comment but does not need congressional approval. It is part of a long-running push by Obama and federal agencies to close the wide gap between men's and women's pay. The commission's proposal would not require companies to disclose the specific salaries of individual employees, but it would seek aggregate data on pay ranges and hours worked. “The goal is to help businesses that are trying to do the right thing ... to get a clearer picture of how they can make sure their employees are being treated equally,” Obama said at a White House event. title: Republicans say Trump's deal with Democrats complicates tax reform
text: U.S. Republican lawmakers warned on Friday that President Donald Trump's legislative deal with Democrats to aid hurricane victims and keep the government funded for another three months could complicate his next major priority, tax reform. Trump's abrupt change of strategy gives a clear win to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi, and that could slow the Republicans' legislative agenda, they said. “This kind of creates complications relative to tax reform,” said Representative Ryan Costello of Pennsylvania. “It seems to me that there’s an element of unpredictability from one issue to the next and this week is sort of a reflection of that.” “There was a lot of work going into how this was going to take shape in September. And that was entirely undermined … seemingly very spontaneously.” After Trump's deal with Democratic leaders, the House of Representatives on Friday passed legislation providing $15.25 billion in emergency disaster aid for victims of Hurricane Harvey, which battered coastal areas of Texas and Louisiana last week, and of Hurricane Irma, which is expected to hit Florida in the coming days. The deal, already approved by the Senate on Thursday, also raises the U.S. government's debt ceiling and lets it keep funding federal spending programs until Dec. 8, the new deadline for an agreement on both issues. But some Republicans worry that Democrats will be able to use their negotiating leverage in early December to resist changes on key tax issues, especially the corporate tax rate, which Trump wants to cut from 35 percent to 15 percent. Republican Senator Ben Sasse said watching Trump empower Democrats had been “embarrassing” for a Republican-controlled Congress and that the deal made Schumer “the most powerful man in America.”

title: Watch Trump Fans Attack Peaceful Protesters Holding ‘America’s Already Great’ Sign
text: Two completely peaceful protesters were attacked and forcibly removed from a Donald Trump rally on Monday after loyal supporters realized their signs were pro-Obama and anti-Trump. The rally in Lowell, Massachusetts was packed, and the footage shows two men in glasses sitting among the supporters. The men aren't doing anything to draw attention to themselves other than holding bright yellow signs, one reading "America is already great" and another saying "God bless President Obama". Eventually, Trump's fans figure out that the two are on the opposite side of the voting spectrum. Once they discover this, a few of Trump's loyal and aggressive minions try to start a verbal altercation with the protesters. When that didn't work, the Trump lovers took it a step further. The supporters grabbed the signs out of the non-confrontational protesters' hands and ripped them to shreds as many other nearby supporters began screaming and chanting Trump's name. Before long, security surrounded the two men and escorted them out of the rally. Trump can be heard talking over the noise, saying "Friend or foe, I don't know" as he notices the commotion. The video of the incident was posted by YouTube user Harrison Walsh.
